ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS 
Setting up of rooftop helipads 
 
*261. SHRI DHARAM PAL SABHARWAL:†† 
 SHRI N.R. GOVINDARAJAR: 
Will the Minister of CIVIL AVIATION be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is mandatory to seek approval of Director General, Civil Aviation (DGCA) 
construction of rooftop helipads; 
(b) if so, the details of guidelines in this regard; 
(c) the names of individuals/companies who have been gi ven permission to construct 
rooftop helipads in Mumbai and Delhi; and 
(d) the number of applications pending, with names of corporate houses/individuals? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF CIVIL AVIATION (SHRI PRAFUL 
PATEL): (a) to (d) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House.  
 Statement  
(a)Yes, Sir. 
(b)Guidelines for heliport planning, physical chara cteristics, infrastructure, markings, 
safety services etc. are given in the Civil Aviation Requirements (CAR) Section 4 Series B 
Part III dated 28.08.2006 on the subject of "Helipo rt" and guidelines for application are 
given in the Civil Aviation Requirement Section 4 Series F Part! dated 16.10.2006. These 
guidelines are available on the DGCA website. 
(c)Operational authorisation has been given to M/s. Essar Group, Mumbai and  M/s Taj 
Wellington Mews, Mumbai for helicopter operations from their roof top Airports. 
(d)Ten proposals for elevated rooftop heliports are pending and they are: 
(i) M/s. Aditya Birla Memorial Hospital, Pune; (ii)  United Breweries (Holdings) 
Ltd.,    Bangalore; (iii) M/s. Satnam Realtors Pvt.  Ltd., Mumbai; (iv) M/s. Bai 
Kabibai & 
Hansraj Morarji Charity Trust, Mumbai; (v) M/s. KKJ Foundation, Ernaculam, Kerala; 
(vi) M/s. G-Corp Project Pvt. Ltd., Bangalore; (vii) Jai Prakash Narayan Apex Trauma 
Centre, AIIMS, New Delhi; (viii) M/s. Devi Construction Company Civil Engineers &       
Builders, Pune and (ix) M/s. Brigade Enterprises Ltd., Bangalore (two proposals). 
†† The question was actually asked on the floor of the House by Shri Dharam Pal Sabharwal.

SHRI N.R. GOVINDARAJAR: Sir, I would like to ask th e hon. Minister whether the 
Government asked the public sector undertaking, Paw an Hans, to prepare the feasibility 
report on construction of heliports and helipads in the country. If so, what are the details of 
the feasibility report submitted by the Pawan Hans? 
SHRI PRAFUL PATEL: Sir, I appreciate the spirit of the question. The biggest problem 
we face today is, on the one side, we want these se rvices to expand; everybody feels that 
helicopter transportation, even in case of medical emergencies or otherwise, is very important. 
And, on the other side, unfortunately, if you see, except the airports of Mumbai or Delhi or 
any other major airport, in any major metropolitan city, there is virtually not a single heliport 
or piece of land available for use of helicopter operations. And, that is why Pawan Hans has 
been trying, it may have been read by you also in t he media, to develop heliports in Delhi 
and in other cities. Unfortunately, we have not yet  met with any success because land 
availability is with local administration and they should provide for all these things. Ultimately, 
it is a service to the people of that city or that region. So, I would urge, in fact, all the hon. 
Members also to take it up with their respective ar eas and provide this thing. It is not for 
Pawan Hans; it could be used by anybody. It is impo rtant because in this day and age, for 
medical evacuation and other kinds of emergencies, helicopter is considered a very, very 
reliable mode of transport. 
SHRI B.J. PANDA: Sir, as the hon. Minister is aware, I speak with a little bit of experience 
of general aviation and particularly of helicopters, he has earned many compliments for the 
opening up of the aviation sector and the very rapid growth. I would like to submit to him 
that our regulations — not just for heliports, but for general aviations a whole — are in need 
of a complete overhaul because many of them were dr afted many decades ago and the 
technologies and realities have changed. Sir, I am also aware that he is working on some 
such programme. I have met some of his officers. He has got some very enthusiastic people 
in the DGCA and I know that they are doing some benchmarking exercises with international 
norms. I would like the hon. Minister to apprise us, what is the status of this benchmarking 
exercise? And, can you give us any commitment as to what timeframe in which you can have 
an overhaul of these regulations so that they are in line with international norms? 
SHRI PRAFUL PATEL: What Mr. Panda has just mentioned. Sir, he himself is a helicopter 
pilot. He recently acquired a license from South Af rica and also endorsed by the Indian 
DGCA. So, I am sure, he has a very close interactio n with the regulatory authorities. Sir, 
again I repeat, all basic guidelines, rules and regulations are framed inaccordance with the 
International Civil Aviation Organisation. They hav e a Charter. We are a signatory to the 
Charter and we are following those guidelines. Of c ourse, aviation in India has changed 
substantially in the last few years and to that ext ent we need to update and do a lot of 
homework to make our rules and regulations in sync with what is the requirement of the day. 
I can assure you that not only is this an on-going exercise, even last week this hon. House 
passed the Aircraft Amendment Bill which seeks cert ain more regulatory powers to the 
regulator. Earlier, so many things, like licensing of airports and various other things including 
technicians, engineers, etc. were not so much in th e purview of the DGCA. But now, we 
have brought in that amendment so that all these th ings can be addressed. Also, just to 
finally highlight, we have in close cooperation a M emorandum of Understanding with the 
USFAA, which is the Federal Aviation Authority, and also with the European EASA and we 

4    Oral Answers [RAJYA SABHA] to Questions  
are now working closely to devise procedures becaus e earlier our aviation was of a very 
smaller scale and now with the high growth, we need to factor in all these changes to make 
aviation not only safe and secure but also to factor the concerns raised by him. 
DR. KARAN SINGH: Sir, apart from the roof-top heliport, which certainly is a welcome 
addition, I would like to point out that in the mountainous areas of our country, particularly 
in the North-East and in Himachal Pradesh, Jammu and Kashmir and Uttaranchal, there are 
areas which are not accessible at all, and there is  no space to build airports. Is there any 
programme with the Ministry to build a series of he liports? I think, you don't need a lot of 
land. If you build a series of heliports and introd uce helicopter services, it will greatly 
expedite the movement of people, tourists and other  essential services in the mountainous 
areas. Is the any such plan under your consideration? 
SHRI PRAFUL PATEL: Sir, certainly, helicopter is the simplest and possibly the fastest 
mode of travel in such kind of terrains. We have a large terrain in our country. Many States 
are virtually in the hilly terrain or mountainous t errain. Therefore, it is advisable to have 
more helicopter activity. I do admit that we have g ot a lot of requests from many State 
Governments. Our endeavour, of course, is to see th at the State-owned Pawan Hans does 
the maximum operation. But it is not possible for t he only company in the State sector to 
support this kind of initiative. To that extent, a lot more private companies have now been 
given licences. They are operating in these areas. Of course, they are not to the entire 
satisfaction of all of us or able to meet the requirements of that region, but, again, heliports, 
I would say, can be provided by each State Government in many places. Ultimately, there is 
no construction. It is a paved piece of concrete which requires a couple of acres and a little 
clearance around it. I am sure, if the State Governments really take this up, as an initiative, 
and also lower the sales-tax on the fuel for this kind of operations, this will become a little bit 
practical; otherwise, helicopter operations are muc h more expensive than fix-swing 
operations. If fuel is more expensive, naturally, it will add to the cost of operations. It will not 
make it a means of more people travelling in it. So, it is a combination of providing a little bit 
of infrastructure support and a little bit of incentive. I am sure, the State Governments would 
come forward. Everything can't be done by us. We can only be the catalyst for growth. We 
can only be the facilitator. A little bit of respon sibility should be taken up by the State 
Governments also. I would urge upon the hon. Members also to help us in this endeavour. 
SHRI S.S. AHLUWALIA: Sir, the demand for roof-top helipads and heliports are growing 
day by day, especially, from the corporate sector a nd new colonies or new satellite towns 
which are coming up. The new builders, when they an nounce a swimming pool, they talk 
about heliports and helipad facilities in their bui lding. The point is that while drafting the 
guidelines, though he has already stated that it is  done as per the international guidelines, 
whether the air freedom of the cities is taken into  consideration. In a city, if you allow a 
person in a multi-soreyed building to construct a h elipad, you are obstructing the 
neighbouring area. You need an open area for that. But in a highly dense city like Mumbai, 
Kolkata, Chennai, Bangalore and Hyderabad where, maybe, a rich-man is asking for helipad 
on the roof-top and if you are permitting him, you are creating a nuisance for the neighbours. 
I would like to know whether you have taken that into consideration or not. 
Secondry, I have noted that in most of the districts, whenever a VVIP visits that district, 
they make a temporary helipad. If a helipad mapping is done-just now my learned colleague. 
Dr. Karan Singh, has mentioned about hilly areas—it  will be useful simultaneously for any 
other medical emergency or for any other emergency and the GPRS system should be

*262. SHRI RAVULA CHANDRA SEKAR REDDY: Will the Minister of FINANCE be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government is increasing the credit flow fr om commercial banks to the 
Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises (MSMEs); 
(b) if so, the details thereof during the last three years. State-wise; 
(c) whether Government has any proposal to give special packages to each State in this 
regard, especially in Andhra Pradesh; 
(d) if so, the details thereof; 
(e) the present position thereof; and 
(f) if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF FINANCE (SHRI R CHIDAMBARAM): (a) to (f) A Statement is laid 
on the Table of the House. 
Statement  
(a) to (f) For stepping up credit to Small and Medium Enterprises (SMEs), Government of 
India had announced a Policy Package in Parliament on August 10,2005 advising all Scheduled

Sector for the year'2006-07 over the year 2005-06. The present data collecting system of

SHRI RAVULA CHANDRA SEKAR REDDY: Sir, the question pertains to Micro, Small and 
Medium Enterprises. I wanted to know from the hon. Minister about the problems being faced by 
the Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises, more particularly the small-scale industries. The small scale 
industry is facing a stiff competition and is in a difficult situation. They have to counter the MNCs and 
other big companies and many of them are on the verge of collapse. I want to know from the hon. 
Minister about special incentives for their revival, like reducing the interest rate, tax and power tariff, 
etc. so that they can sustain. Is there any proposal? The answer is, "There is no such package". I 
request the Government to consider this demand of incentives. I need a specific answer. 
SHRI PAWAN KUMAR BANSAL: Sir, after appreciating the difficulties being faced by the SMEs, 
in August, 2005, this Government had announced its intention to double the credit to the SMEs in 
five years. I am happy to report that the progress is better than that. The year-on-year growth is 25 per 
cent, instead of 20 per cent. Further, as the hon. Member and the hon. House know, the Credit 
Guarantee Fund Trust has also been set up, where one time guarantee fee has been reduced from 2.5 per 
cent to 1.5 per cent. Then the Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises Development Act was enacted by 
Parliament in the year 2006. There was a scheme for one-time settlement also which was in force up to 
31st March, 2006. Sir, all possible assistance to the SMEs has been extended by the Government 
and the banking sector. 
Sir, the definition has been changed. Now we have also included the micro enterprises, which 
face a greater difficulty. Micro enterprises, small enterprises and the medium enterprises are all included 
in the priority sector, and the public sector banks are obliged to lend up to 40 per cent of the total 
adjusted net bank credit to the priority sector. So, this section comes under the priority sector. 
SHRl RAVULA CHANDRA SEKAR REDDY: Sir, my second supplementary may not be directly 
related to this Ministry. But there is a lengthy procedure in getting clearances for establishing a 
small unit at the suburban level, and by virtue of closure, many people are rendered jobless. And 
since unemployment is growing in the country, to sustain the small scale industries and to help the 
people, who are working in such industries, what is the package available for them? 
SHRI PAWAN KUMAR BANSAL: Sir, firstly, there is a decision to set up a specialised SSI 
branch, at least one branch, of the banks in every district. That is one decision which has been 
taken. Then, the collateral requirement, for loans up to Rs. 5 lakhs, has been

ceased as far lending to the SSI sector is concerne d. And the banks have been advised to 
consider increasing the exemption limit, for obtaining collateral security for all micro and 
small party accounts, from the existing Rs. 25 lakhs to Rs. 50 lakhs, and the collateral-free 
loan, up to Rs.50 lakhs, is covered for guarantee under the new Credit Guarantee Scheme for 
micro and small enterprises. Also, the loan applica tion for credit limit up to Rs. 25,000 is 
cleared within a fortnight. Loan applications above  Rs. 25,000 are cleared within eight 
weeks so that time is not wasted in that and the pr oject does not lose its viability. It was 
keeping in view the changes in the emerging economi c scenario and the trends, and 
considering that there is increase in the minimum viable scale of the enterprises, that these 
initiatives were taken, and there was a paradigm shift in the definition of the SME sector as 
well.

DR. K. MALAISAMY: Sir, according to the reply, ther e has been growth in credit to 
industries. While we appreciate this, we would like  to know the share of the small scale 
industries in that. They say there is growth of credit to industry. But, with reference to the 
overall growth of credit to industry, what is the percentage of credit to small-scale industries? 
That is one point. The second point is.. 
MR. CHAIRMAN: One question only. 
DR. K. MALAISAMY: He will reply to it in one stroke. Now, I can speak with certain 
authority here because, in the Standing committee on Industry, we had convened a meeting 
of industries' association on the one side and the public sector banks on the other. We 
toured the length and breadth of the country; we di scussed it in the committee. Sir, the 
points raised by the associations of the industries are that the rate of interest for the Small 
Scale Industry are very much higher than the rate of interest levied on the large scale. What 
I am trying to ask is, in spite of the Parliamentar y Standing committee's recommendation 
that they should take a special stand to reduce the rate of interest, as far as the Small scale 
Industry is concerned, what decision they have taken, in this regard. They are trying to say 
that they are instructing the commercial banks, etc. It is not going to help us at all. Will there 
be a specific diktat from the Ministry that the Small Scale Industry should be given loan at 
lesser rate of interest. 

10    Oral Answers [RAJYA SABHA] to Questions  
SHRI PAWAN KUMAR BANSAL: Sir, the first part is regarding the percentage of the 
total net bank credit. As far as the SMEs is concerned, it is 14 per cent; and then in the case of 
the Small Scale Industry, it is 8 per cent. When it  conies to the interest, I had mentioned 
earlier, sir, that the present rate of interest for the Small Scale Industry is the BPLR, i.e., the 
benchmark, prime lending rate of the bank, i.e.. plus-minus two per cent. Sir, the rate is fixed 
by banks. It differs slightly from bank to bank in every case. But, that is the normal thing 
which is done. Up to two lakhs, it has not to excee d the BPLR. Those are the guidelines 
which are being followed.

policy change were directed towards overseas deriva tive investments and FIIs and their 
sub-accounts shall not issue, renew ODIs with under  lying as derivatives with immediate 
effect and were required to wind up the current position over 18 months. Further issuance of 
ODIs for the sub-accounts of FIIs will be discontinued with immediate effect; they are required 
to wind up the current position over 18 months. FIIs who were currently issuing ODIs with 
notional value of PNs outstanding as a percentage of the assets under control in India of less 
than 40 per cent shall be allowed to issue further ODIs only at the incremental rate of 5 per 
cent of their assets under control. Then, those FII s with notion value of PNs outstanding 
excluding derivatives as a percentage of their AMC in India for more than 40 per cent shall 
issued PNs only against cancellation, redemption of closing out of the existing PNs. These 
decisions were taken by the market regulator having regard to the situation in the market and 
its response to the inflows in to the capital market.

SHRI RAVI SHANKAR PRASAD: Sir, I am grateful to you for allowing me to speak. The 
hon. Finance Minister, may I take on the reply that  you have just given? The National 
Security Advisor is on record having said about the influence of these elements in the stock 
market. How much I should take it from your stand just now of suspected' and his categorical 
stand, I leave it to your judgement. But my question is on a more fundamental issue. There is 
a question on the ban on PN notes. Would you kindly  come clean as to why the PN was 
permitted-and what went on in the stock market-why need arose to ban it? What were the 
compelling circumstances, which led to the banning of it, and what has been after-effect 
thereof? I would like to know it. 
SHRI P. CHIDAMBARAM: Sir, participatory notes are i n vogue for many years. The 
point is that the participatory notes are issued based on underlying assets as well as on the 
basis of derivative instruments. What SEBI has done  in October is to place restrictions on 
the issue of participatory notes with the underlyin g as derivatives. As I read out and I will 
read it out again, this is what SEBI did. "In respe ct of overseas derivative investments, the 
following four .steps will be taken. The FII in the sub-accounts shall not issue any ODIs with 
underlying derivatives and they are required to wind up iheir position in 18 months. Issuance 
of ODIs by sub-accounts will be discontinued and th ey will wind up their current position 
over 18 months. FIIs, who currently issue ODIs with  notional values of PNs outstanding 
excluding derivatives, but if it is less than 40 per cent, FII can only issue it at an incremental 
rate of 5 per cent. If it was already more than 40 per cent, FII cannot issue any PNs unless it 
is against cancellation/redemption. So, there is no  absolute ban on PNs. One kind of PNs, 
which are based on derivatives, are being regulated, capped and they are being requested to 
wind down over a period of 18 months. There is no absolute ban on participatory notes.

Task force for interlinking of rivers 
†*268.    SHRI KRISHAN LAL BALMIKI:†† 
SHRI KALRAJ MISHRA:  
Will the Minister of WATER RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the Task Force constituted for interlinking Of rivers has been 
dissolved; 
(b) if so, the reasons therefor; 
(c) the suggestions of the Task Force in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF WATER RESOURCES (SHRI JAI 
PRAKASH NARAYAN YADAV); (a) to (c) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement  
(a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) Task force submitted Action Plan I and Action Plan II in April, 2003 and April, 2004 
respectively and thus completed its assigned function. 
(c) Recommendations of Task Force: 
(0 Task Force got prepared Terms of Reference (TOR)  for preparation of Detailed 
Project Reports (DPR) through M/s Engineers India L td. (EIL) for providing 
guidance on norms of appraisal of individual projects. 
(ii) On the issue of suitable mechanism for bringing about speedy consensus amongst 
the States, Task Force has suggested meeting at the  highest level to agree after 
the technical-level discussions with emphasis that outstanding issues should be 
such that they can  be addressed in Detailed Project Report stage. 
(iii) The Task Force has stated that the peninsular  links are the right components to 
begin with as the Himalayan links have internationa l implications and it is too 
early to pursue the matter as ILR is a concept and not a single project. Top priority 
links identified by Task Force on Interlinking of Rivers are as under: 
(a) Ken-Betwa link UP&MP 
(b) Parbati-Kalisindh-Chambal link     MP & Rajasthan 
(iv) On the basis of reprot from IIM-Ahmedabad, a two tier institutional/organizational 
set up has been suggested for the implementation of the programme on interlinking 
of Rivers (ILR) with an apex body of the proposed set up. 
† .Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
†† The question as actually asked on the floor of the House by Shri Krishan Lal Balmiki. 

20    Oral Answers [RAJYA SABHA] to Questions  
(v) Task Force on Interlinking of Rivers consulted ICIICI for funding options. ICICI 
has proposed that funding should be partly through public, public-private and 
private inputs. 
Based on NWDA studies, National Council of Applied Economic Research 
(NCAER) has estimated that the cost of ILR project would be Rs. 4.44 Lakh crore. 
NCAER is of the view that the programme would take nearly35-40 years.

Supply of LPG in the Country  
 †*263.    SHRI SATYAVRAT CHATURVEDI: 
SHRI MOTILAL VORA: 
Will the Minister of PETROLEUM AND NATURAL GAS be pleased to state: 
(a) the names of those States in the country, in respect of which Government is aware of 
shortage of LPG therein; 
(b) the quantum of LPG being allocated in the counry, State-wise; and 
(c) whether allocation of LPG for those States would be  enhanced in the current year, 
where such allocation is not done as per their requirement? 
THE MINISTER OF PETROLEUM AND NATURAL GAS (SHRI MURLI DEORA): (a) to 
(c) Public Sector Oil Marketing Companies (OMCs) have reported that at present, there is no 
overall shortage of LPG in the country, and LPG supplies to distributors are being made by 
the OMCs through indigenous production and imports in accordance with the requirement 
of customers registered with the LPG distributors. However, OMCs have from time to time 
reported occasional backlogs in certain States/Unio n Territories due to natural calamities 
such as floods, road breaches, collapse of bridge and stoppage of work by various sections 
of employees, transporters and contract labourers, hartals etc. The Government has advised 
OMCs to liquidate the backlog in the States/UTs by operating the bottling plants on holidays 
& by extending hours of working. 
The demand of the customers is met by the OMCs and they have supplied 4.86 million 
metric tonnes (MMT) of LPG in the country during the period from April-September, 2007 as 
against 4.65 MMT during the period April-September, 2006, showing a growth rate of 4.5%. 
State-wise details of LPG supplied during the period April-September, 2007 are given in the 
Statement.

Participation of Private Sector in Training of Pilots  
*269. SHRI KALRAJ MISHRA:             
SHRI SANTOSH BAGRODLA: 
Will the Minister of CIVIL AVIATION be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the Ministry has made an assessment of prospective need for commercial pilots 
in civil aviation sector in the country; 
(b) if so, whether the country has world class training  institutes to meet the prospective 
requirement of trained commercial pilots; 
(c) the current strength of the existing civil aviation academies/campuses in the country; 
(d) whether Government propose to enhance the existing strength of aviation academics/ 
campuses; and 
(e) what will be the cost of such expansion and whether Government is open to participation by the 
private operators? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF CIVIL AVIATION (SHRI PRAFUL 
PATEL): (a) Yes, Sir. With the present growth of aviation industry it has been estimated that in the 
next five years 5000 additional pilots would be required for scheduled operations and 1000 pilots 
for non scheduled and private operations. 
(b) Yes, Sir. There is a premier flying training institute, namely, Indira Gandhi Rashtriya Uran 
Akademi (IGRUA) at Rae Bareli in Uttar Pradesh. It has also been decided to set up a world class 
flying training institute at Gondia, Maharashtra. 
(c) There are 43 flying training institutes in the country approved by Directorate General of 
Civil Aviation (DGCA) providing training for variou s licences like Private Pilot Licence, 
Commercial Pilot Licence etc. The Indira Gandhi Rashtriya Uran Akademi (IGRUA) is an 
autonomous society under the Central Government. Of the remaining 42 institutes, 27 are run by 
various State Governments and the balance 15 by private entrepreneurs. Out of the 43 approved 
flying clubs, 16 are non-operational. At present approximately 850 cadets are undergoing flying 
training for various courses at these institutions. 
† Original notice of the question was received in Hindi.

(d) Yes, Sir. The Government has taken various steps to  strengthen the flying clubs. 
These include upgradation and modernisation of trai ning infrastructure of Indira Gandhi 
Rashtriya Uran Akademi (IGRUA) to enhance its train ing capacity, setting up of a world 
class flying training institute at Gondia, Maharash tra and assistance to flying clubs by 
allocating trainer aircraft through the Directorate  General of Civil Aviation/Aero Club of 
India (ACI). 
(e) For IGRUA, which is under the administrative control of this Ministry, the Government 
has approved two schemes for upgradation viz. development of civil and electrical 
infrastructure and acquisition of trainer aircrafts costing Rs. 21.82 crore and Rs. 43.10 crore 
respectively. The Government has also proposed to incur an expenditure of Rs. 108.07 crore 
for development of Birsi aerodrome for setting up of flying training institute at Gondia. An 
amount of Rs. 12.03 crore for purchase of trainer aircrafts to be allocated by ACI to various 
flying clubs has also been approved. 
Private operators are already in the field of train ing of pilots. It has been decided to 
develop the flying training institute at Gondia as a Joint Venture Company under the aegis of 
Airports Authority of India with a private flying training organisation of international repute 
as Joint Venture Partner. It has also been decided to develop IGRUA as a world class flying 
training institute through management contract arrangement with flying training organisation 
of international repute.

PATEL): (a) to (d) Directorate General of Civil Aviation (DGCA) has issued Civil Aviation

within a region, expand air travel services for Tie r II and III cities and between specific

(0    Airlines operating with aircraft with take off mass equal to or exceeding 40,000kg. 
(1) upto 3 aircraft—Rs 30 crores. 
(2) for each additional aircraft, additional equity investment of Rs. 10 crores will 
be required, subject to a miximum of Rs. 50 crores after which no further 
equity enhancement is required.

(1) upto 3 aircraft—Rs 12 crores

There may be no need for further enhancement of equ ity if the paid up 
equity/reserves of Rs. 50. crores is available with the airline.

(a) whether it is a fact historical monuments continue to be defaced inspite of framing of 
guidelines; 
(b) if so, the reasons therefor; and 
(c) what steps are being taken to protect these historical monuments? 
THE MINISTER OF CULTURE (SHRIMATI AMBIKA SONI): (a) and (b) There are 
instances of scribing and graffiti on walls in some monuments due to lack of awareness and 
ignorance of the value of our cultural heritage among the general public. 
(c) Periodic awareness programmes are organized at the monuments from time to time by 
involving public as well as students. The watch and  ward staff have been asked to be 
vigilant in order to detect such acts of vandalism and the supervisory staff instructed to 
undertake regular inspections. In addition the regular watch and ward staff, private security 
personnel, State police guards and CISF have also been provided for the safety and security 
of selected monuments. Media Campaign for raising the awareness has also been launched. 
Besides the above, penalty clauses exist in the Anc ient Monuments and Archaeological 
Sites and Remains Act, 1958 in which such acts are punishable by imprisonment of 3 months 
or with a fine of Rs. 5000/- or both.

Short-term credit to big companies 
 †l522.    SHRI RAVI SHANKAR PRASAD: 
SHRI RAJ MOHINDER SINGH MAJITHA: 
Will the Minister of FINANCE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that short-term credit to big companies by Public Sector Banks in 
the country is provided at the rate of 7.5 to 9 percent whereas the Prime Lending Rate is 12.75 
to 13.25 percent. 
(b) if not, the details thereof; and 
(c) the categories of companies treated by bank as big companies? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (SHRI PAWAN KUMAR 
BANSAL): (a) and (b) Effective from October 18,1994, the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has 
deregulated the interest rates on advances above Rs . 2 lakhs, including the housing loans 
and these interest rates are determined by the bank s themselves with the approval of their 
Board of Directors subject to Benchmark Prime Lendi ng Rates (BPLR) and spread guide 
lines. In order to enhance transparency in banks' pricing of their loan products, banks have 
been advised to fix their BPLR after taking into account (i) actual cost of funds, (ii) operating 
expenses and (iii) a minimum margin to cover regulatory requirement of provisioning/capital 
charge and profit margin and ensure that the BPLR truly reflects the actual cost. Individual 
banks, therefore, determine interest rates to be ch arged to a particular borrower subject to 
BPLR and spread guidelines. Given the prevailing cr edit market in India and the need to 
continue with concessionality for small borrowers, the practice of treating BPLR as the 
ceiling for loans upto Rs. two lakhs continues. However, Banks are free to determine the rates 
of interest without reference to BPLR and regardles s of the size in respect of loans of 
purchase of consumer durables, loans to individuals  against shares and debentures/bonds, 
other non-priority sector personal loans, etc. 
RBI had stated that the outcome for interest rates depends mainly on the outlook for 
inflation, growth procpects and investment demand a nd it is not possible to predict short-
run movements in interest rates. Data on BPLR and S ub-BPLR lending of PSBs are as

†1524. SHRI BANWARI LAL KANCHHAL: Will the Minister of FINANCE be pleased to

imposed at the rate of 20 per cent of sale price;

on arbitrary basis;

of Capital Gains Tax on circle rate has come into force;

immovable properties by not fully disclosing the sale consideration, law was amended by the 
Finance Act, 2002 so as to provide that in a case where the sale consideration of an immovable 
property declared by the seller is less than the value adopted by Stamp Valuation Authority 
for the purpose of payment of stamp duty, such valu e shall be deemed to be the sale 
consideration.

property is less than the value adopted by Stamp Valuation Authority, a safeguard has been 
provided in the law to mitigate the hardship. In such situations, the Assessing Officer may 
refer the valuation of the property to the Valuation Officer.

Amendment of RDBAct, 1993 
1532. SHRI KAMAL AKHTAR: Will the Minister of FINANCE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government has studied the Supreme Court's order that Co-operative Banks cannot 
take recourse to debt recovery under the Recovery o f Debts due to Banks and Financial 
Institutions Act (RDB Act), 1993; 
(b) if so, whether Government would amend the Act so that these Co-operative Banks shall also 
be included within the provisions of the Act; 
(c) if so, by when; 
(d) if not, the reasons therefor; 
(e) the reasons for Government retreating on promise made on 6th December, 2006 in the house to 
bring a comprehensive bill to amend banking regulation act to remove dual control in Cooperative 
Banks; and 
(f) by when the bill would be introduced? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (SHRI PAWAN KUMAR 
BANSAL): (a) to (d) Yes, Sir. In separate matters coming up before the High Courts of Mumbai 
and Andhra Pradesh it was held by them that a Tribunal constituted under the provisions of the 
Recovery of Debts due to Banks and Financial Institutions Act, 1993 has exclusive jurisdiction, to 
entertain and decide applications from a Co-operative Bank for recovery of debts due to such a 
bank. Further, it was also held that courts and authorities under the State Co-operative Societies Act 
as also The Multi-state Co-operative Societies Act, 2002 would cease to have jurisdiction to 
entertain the applications submitted by the Cooperative Banks for recovery of their dues. Aggrieved 
by the above, a bunch of appeals/ Special Leave Petitions were field in the Supreme Court of India 
where the matter of applicability of Recovery of Debts due to Banks and Financial Institutions Act, 
1993 to the Cooperative Banks established under the State Co-operative Societies Act of Maharashtra 
2002 was referred by the Chief Justice of India to a three judge bench. 
Reversing the judgement of the High Court, the Supreme Court held that the provisions of Debts 
due to Banks and Financial Institutions Act, 1993 are not applicable to the recovery of dues by the Co-
operatives from their members. However, the provisions of the State Co-operative Societies Act and 
Multi-state Cooperative Societies Act, 2002 would continue to be applicable for recovery of dues by 
the Cooperative Banks. As these observations of

the Supreme Court are in line with the request made by the petitioner Cooperative Banks in 
their appeal petitions, this order of the Supreme Court is not likely to place the Cooperative 
Banks in any disadvantageous position for purpose of recovery of their dues. 
Cooperative Banks can also take recourse to provisi ons of Securitisation and 
Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act, 2002 for 
recovery of their dues. There is no proposal to amend the RDB Act 1993. 
(e) and (f) As UCBs are subjected to dual control b y the RBI and the respective State

(ii)   Facilitating human resource development and IT initiatives in UCBs. 
(iii)   Professionalisation of Audit i.e.   statutory audit  by Chartered Accountant for

(iv)   Putting in place fit and proper criteria for the Chief Executive Officers based on the 
guidelines of the bank. 
Consequent upon signing of MoU, a State Level Task Force for UCBs (TAFCUB) has 
been constituted for 13 States. These States constitute majority of the UCBs. The TAFCUB 
consists of representation from RBI, State Government and UCBs. 
Further, the Government has approved a revival package to strengthen Short-Term Rural

Financial assistance for STCCS under the package is available for cleansing of Balance

Mismanagement of Micro Finance Scheme 
1561. SHRl SHAHID SUDDIQUI: Will the Minister of FINANCE be pleased to state: 
(a) what action is being taken to make the "Micro Finance Scheme" more transparent and 
people friendly in view of mismanagement being repo rted from all quarters on the said 
scheme; and 
(b) what is the percentage of total loan being given by  the Nationalized Banks through 
the Ministry? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (SHRI PAWAN KUMAR 
BANSAL): (a) and (b) The Self Help Groups (SHGs)- Bank Linkage Programme has emerged 
as the major Micro Finance programme in the country , which is being implemented by 
Commercial Banks, Regional rural Banks and Cooperat ive Banks. As on March 31,2007, 
29.24 lakh SHGs have been linked to banks involving a total credit flow of Rs. 18,040 crore 
(cumulative figure since 1992). Similarly, under Swaranjayanti Gram Swarozgar Yojana (SGSY), 
43551 SHGs were disbursed loan amounting to Rs. 26,150.74 lakh, which is 64% of the total 
loan disbursed under the scheme, during the year 2006-07. The Nationalized Banks have a 
predominant share in the lending under this scheme. 
Banks have been advised that micro credit should fr om an integral part of the bank's 
corporate credit plan and should be reviewed at the highest level on a quarterly basis. They 
have also been advised to focus on relatively less banked areas, engage in capacity building 
and empowerment of the groups to the desired extent  and adhere to their system and 
practices and lending policies with a view to ensure better transparency and people friendly 
practices.  
The Government of India has introduced the Micro Financial Sector (Development and 
Regulation) Bill, 2007 on 20th March, 2007 in the L ok Sabha, which envisages a formal 
statutory framework for the promotion, development and regulation of the micro finance 
sector.

1584. SHRI MOINUL HASSAN: Will the Minister of PETROLEUM AND NATURAL 
GAS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether RIL is a contractor selling gas Krishna Godavari (KG) Basin owned by Union 
of India; 
(b) whether Article 39(b) of the Constitution directs t he State that the ownership and 
control of material resource of community are so di stributed as based to sub-serve the 
common good; 
(c) if so, whether Government is aware that the RIL gas pricing will have adverse impact 
on price of power and fertilizer; and 
(d) if so, the reaction of Government? 
THE MINISTER OF PETROLEUM AND NATURAL GAS (SHRI MURLI DEORA):(a) 
and (b) By virtue of Article 297 of the Constitutio n of India, petroleum in its natural state 
lying in the geographical territory, territorial wa ters and the continental shelf of India and 
the Exclusive Economic Zone of India is vested in the Government. The Government enters 
into Production Sharing Contracts (PSC) with the co ntractor to invest and explore for 
hydrocarbons in the contract area under NELP. If hy drocarbons are discovered and 
commercially produced, contractor is entitled to recover the investment made and share the 
profit with the Government as per the provisions of PSC. 
(c) and (d) Government constituted an Empowered Group of Ministers (EGoM) to consider 
issues relating to pricing and commercial utilization of natural gas under NELP. EGoM has 
decided the issue of pricing of gas under NELP. In terms of the provisions of the Production 
Sharing Contracts, contractors have the freedom to sell gas in the domestic market at arms 
length prices to the benefit of parties to the cont ract. While approving the pricing formula, 
the EGoM has taken care to protect the interest of gas consuming sector against persistent 
rise in international crude prices, by imposing a c eiling of USS 60 on the crude price per 
barrel in the formula.

1595. SHRI KUMAR DEEPAK DAS: Will the Minister of PETROLEUM AND NATURAL 
GAS be pleased to state: 
(a) the fiscal measures being taken to compensate State-run firms for selling fuel below 
cost; and 
(b) whether there is any proposal for price hike on fuel like petrol, diesel, kerosene and 
LPG? 
THE MINISTER OF PETROLEUM AND NATURAL GAS (SHRI MURLI DEORA): 
(a) The Government is partly compensating the Publi c Sector Oil Marketing Companies 
(OMCs) for their under-recoveries resulting form the impact of high international oil prices 
on retail price of sensitive petroleum products. Th e following fiscal measures have been 
taken to compensate OMCs. 
* Issue of Oil Bonds for an amount equal to 42.7% of their under-recoveries accrued from 
sale of sensitive petroleum products. 
*Sharing of under-recoveries by the upstream oil co mpanies by offering discounts on 
crude oil and petroleum products. 
*Rationalisation of taxes and duties on crude oil and sensitive petroluem products. 
(b) As regards pricing of sensitive petroleum products namely petrol, diesel, PDS Kerosene 
and Domestic LPG, Government has been taking all possible measures to ensure that there 
is no hardship to the common man. The Government has adopted the principle of equitable 
burden sharing to protect the interest of common ma n and vulnerable section of society. 
The Government is closely monitoring the internatio nal oil prices and will continue to 
protect the interests of consumers.

with the Ministry of Environment and forests provid ing assistance to various State 
Governments for implementation of pollution abatement works under the National River 
Conservation Plan. Government of Punjab have inform ed that due to urbanization and 
industrialization, pollution is increasing in the rivers passing through the State. In respect 
of Yamnua river, in seven rounds of observations made by the Central Pollution Control 
Board in June-Dec. 2006, the water quality at Palla  was meeting the desired criteria of 
dissolved Oxygen (DO); Biochemical Oxygen Demand (BOD) in three rounds and did not 
meet the criteria in respect of Total Coliform. Water quality did not meet any of these criteria 
in Yamuna at Agra Canal (Madanpur Khadar), Agra Canal (Okhla) and Okhla after- confluence 
with Shahdara drain and Nizamuddin Bridge. As per Government of NCT of Delhi, the water

quality of river Yamuna is meeting the criteria with respect to DO and BOD at palla and, after 
confluence of Najafgarh Drain, it does not meet the criteria of DO, BOD and Coliform. Upper 
Yamuna River Board have informed that Delhi Jal Board have reported from time to time that 
high concentration of ammonia in Yamuna water has b een found at Wazirabad due to 
releases of untreated effluents from Haryana. However, as per the Government of Haryana, 
pollution in river Yamuna is well within the norms when it enters Delhi State and joint 
sampling is done by the State and Central Pollution Control Boards on monthly basis and 
the results are within limits. In respect of river Ghaggar, its waters are polluted by effluents 
discharged from factories located in the various States en route.  
In respect of silting in rivers, Government of Punjab have informed rivers Sutlej, Beas 
and Ravi of Punjab have been tamed by construction of dames with the result that free flow 
of water and accompanying silt in these rivers is minimal. Ghaggar is a seasonal river having 
flash floods and brings a lot of sand/silt. However , as the sand is being mined, there is 
hardly any increase in the net silt load. As per Government of Haryana, there is no trend of 
silt increase in rivers Ghaggar and Yamuna and silt is also removed from river bed through 
different quarries. 
(b) Upper Yamuna River Board have informed that as a result of pollution, the water 
carrying capacity of the river is not affected. Sil ting in rivers is natural phenomena, the 
magnitude of which various from year to year. In view of mining/quarrying of sand/silt, the 
Governments of Punjab and Haryana have indicated th at there is no substantial/adverse 
effect on the carrying capacity of the rivers.

Water surplus to Rajasthan  
1629. SHRI SANTOSH BAGRODIA:               
SHRI MAHMOOD A. MADANI: 
Will the Minister of WATER RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether as per the 1981 agreement for sharing of Ravi-Beas water, there is a provision 
"until such time Rajasthan is in position to utilize its full share, Punjab may utilize the water 
surplus to Rajasthan's requirement"; 
(b) whether Government intends to direct BBMB to restor e remaining 0.60 MAP to 
Rajasthan as Rajasthan is in a position to utilize its full share of 8.6 MAP since 1991; and 
(c) if so, by what specific time, and if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF WATER RESOURCES (SHRI JAY 
PRAKASH NARAYAN YADAV): (a) Yes, Sir. Clause (ii) of the agreement dated 31.12.1981 
among the Chief Ministers of Punjab, Haryana and Rajasthan regarding allocation of surplus 
Ravi-Beas waters provides that until such time as Rajasthan is in a position to utilize its full 
share, Punjab shall be free to utilize the waters surplus to Rajasthan's requirement. 
(b) and (c) Punjab Termination of Agreements Act, 2004, enacted by Punjab Legislature 
on 12.07.04 terminates all agreements on Ravi-Beas waters including the 1981 agreement 
and discharges the State Government from any obligation arising from these agreements. A 
Presidential Reference thereupon is before the Hon'ble Supreme Court. Thus, any direction 
to Bhakra Beas Management Board (BBMB) in the matter of restoration of remaining 0.60 
MAF will depend on the outcome of the Presidential Reference

the submission that 1 wish to make is substantial. It is of significance to the entire Parliament 
and it does really illustrate once again how casually and indifferently the Parliament is being 
treated by the Treasury Benches. I refer. Sir, to an established convention that whenever the 
hon. Prime Minister or the hon. External Affairs Minister undertakes a visit abroad, to any

SHRI JASWANT SINGH: Sir, it is rather like a game of Ludo where you throw wrong and 
go back to start or miss your turn and so on. I don 't want to keep on repeating what I have 
said. But I will repeat the requirement of the Government to inform the Parliament of the visits 
that they undertake to foreign countries. 
Sir, in recent months, the honourable the Prime Min ister, as also the hon. the External 
Affairs Minister, were on visits, of which we are a ware, have been undertaken to various 
countries. The Prime Minister yet again breached a convention which has been the standard 
observed for very long, and I do not remember. Sir,  when it has been breached and I do 
recollect very well reading that the first Prime Minister, hon. Shri Jawaharlal Nehru observed 
the requirement of attending the Parliament and for saking foreign meetings whenever the 
Parliament was in Session. I must say this with great regret that the hon. the Prime Minister 
absented himself in possibly the most crucial week of this Session, for almost a week, when 
the total session is only for three weeks. I am informed — I do not know whether he actually 
went or did not go; it is only newspaper reports that inform me — that he went to Russia. It 
was rather a sudden visit; a 28 hours turn-around visit to Russia. It is quite a record for any 
Indian Prime Minister. Thereafter he came, perhaps,  to change his clothing, and went to 
Singapore. Perhaps, he went there directly; I do not know. He flew to Kampala. There is a 
requirement for us to know of all these events. I say it with great deal of concern, Mr. Deputy 
Chairman, that our neighbourhood is as troubled, and in as great a state of disorder, as I do 
not recollect when it last was. I do not wish to ci te the names of countries; whether it is 
Bangladesh or Nepal, it is in a state of total disg race. So are the events that have happened 
in Pakistan. We recently had a very significant event in Annapolis. Now, what was it? Was it 
a conference for peace or was it a conference to pr epare us for yet another conflict? The 
House has a right to know, Sir. We hear reports of the hon. the Defence Minister, a dear and 
esteemed friend of long standing of mine, who goes to Nathu La and speaks in eulogistic 
lerms of the People's Republic of China's infrastru cture developments. The leader of the 
Congress Party, indeed, undertakes a visit to China  and lauds the systems of China. I do 
hope. Sir, that those systems do not include that we will now start following the methods of 
governance also of China. It is very important that we know; we cannot know unless the

Strike by employees and officers of associate banks of SBI against their merger with 
SBI 
SHRI TAPAN KUMAR SEN (West Bengal): I would like to  draw the attention of the 
House to the strike being observed by 45,000 employees and officers of the associate banks 
of the State Bank of India against the unilateral move of merger of the associate banks with 
the State Bank of India. On this, the employees and officers association has long been airing 
their concerns to the Government, to the Finance Mi nistry and to the respective bank 
managements pertaining to their service conditions,  pertaining to their anxiety over the 
closure of different branches of those banks conseq uent upon merger and consequent 
redundancy, and also the operational necessity of merger at all. I am not going to the issue of 
merger. There may be difference, but I want to draw the attention of the House and also the 
Government towards the fact that bulldozing the concerns of the employees, even for the

Plight of Cotton Growers in Andhra Pradesh  
SHRI RAVULA CHANDRA SEKAR REDDY (Andhra Pradesh): Sir, I am raising an urgent 
issue pertaining to the farmers of Andhra Pradesh S tate, more particularly, the districts of 
Karimnagar, Adilabad, Warangal, Khammam, Nizamabad, Guntur, and Krishna, wherein cotton 
farmers are forced to sell their produce in a distress condition. They are agitating literally on 
the road. The Cotton Corporation of lndia is not at all helping the farmers. In fact, they are 
purchasing cotton from the traders instead of purchasing from the farmers. The activities of 
the Cotton Corporation of India need thorough investigation and inquiry. The farmers are in 
a critical condition. Having grown cotton, the MSP provided for cotton is only Rs.2,060/-. 
But, they are not getting even that amount in the m arket, whereas they are demanding, at 
least, Rs.3,100/- per quintal. As a matter of fact, the Cotton Corporation of India officials are 
taking the commission at the lower level from the middlemen and purchasing cotton from the 
traders, instead of farmers. It has literally become the 'commission corporation of India' in 
Andhra Pradesh. It needs a thorough inquiry. Since long time, they are agitating for MSP. 
Now, the activities of CCl are further creating trouble for the farmers and they are forced to go 
on streets and do all sorts of demonstration. 1 req uest the Government of lndia to enquire 
into the activities of the CCl and to enhance the MSP to Rs.3100/- per quintal, and direct the 
CCI to purchase the cotton from the farmers instead of traders. This is the most urgent and 
important issue. The Government should take note of it and act immediately and in an urgent 
manner.

176   Special [RAJYA SABHA] Mentions  
Concern over poor condition of national highway Shirodi Ghat connecting Mangalore  
SHRI JANARDHANA POOJARY (Karnataka): Sir, the condition of a number of National 
Highways in Karnataka is in very bad shape, particularly, the condition of the Shiradi Ghat 
National Highway is the worst. This road connects B angalore and Mangalore, the two 
important commercial and industrial cities of Karnataka. Over 22 miles of the Shiradi Ghat 
National Highway is in the Ghat section, and is made up of a number of bridges and culverts. 
Thousands of vehicles, both light and heavy, pass through this road day and night, carrying 
people, goods and minerals, either way. 
For over two years, the Shiradi Ghat National Highway is in such a bad condition that the 
vehicular traffic on this road has come to a stand still. This is greatly affecting the commerce 
and industry in and around the two cities. A token repair work undertaken lethargically by 
the State Government out of the Central grant of Rs . 30 crores has not helped. Every day, 
thousands of vehicles are stranded in this section and it takes nearly a day to reach their 
destination, resulting in great inconvenience to women and children. The vehicles now take 
a circuitous route, i.e., either the Bangalore-Char madi Ghat road or the Mysore-Madikeri 
road to traverse between Bangalore and Mangalore. But the condition of even these roads is 
very bad. 
The agitation by the people is turning more violent  each day. I, therefore, appeal to the 
Government to take up the repair work on the Shiradi Ghat National Highway and the Bangalore-
Charmadi Ghat and the Mysore-Madikeri roads on a war-footing. Thank you.

Concern over non-payment of gratuity dues to Garware Nylons workers at Pimpri, Pune 
DR. BARUN MUKHERJEE (West Bengal): Sir, the Garware Nylons Ltd. of Pimpri, Pune 
was shutdown in 1996, thereby throwing 1,200 worker s with 4,000 dependents, to utter 
miseries, almost to the point of starvation death. Regrettably, the company did not pay even 
legitimate dues to these hapless workers till 2003.  They received only 20 per cent of their 
gratuity dues and 18 per cent of other dues in 2003 and 2004 respectively from the official 
Liquidator appointed by the Bombay High Court in 19 98. The workers are still anxiously 
awaiting for payment of rest of their legitimate du es, including gratuity. But, it has been 
reported that the company used/withdrew the gratuit y fund even after official Liquidator 
took over in 1998. It is a matter of serious concern and needs to be probed. 
It has been further reported that the Bombay High Court has been entertaining a person 
posing as the President of the workers' union, who is actually not recognised by the workers 
themselves, to keep gratuity dispute subjudice. It is also a serious matter which needs to be 
probed, along with ascertaining the jurisdiction under the Gratuity Act, 1972. But the burning 
issue is to ensure immediate payment of all gratuit y dues, along with other dues, to the 
starving workers, at least, to relieve part of their sufferings. 
I urge upon the Union Government, particularly the hon. Minister of Corporate Affairs, to 
urgently take all necessary measures to do justice to the deprived workers to ameliorate their 
11-year-long sufferings. 
Need to take steps for prevention of Road Accidents 
SHRI M.V. MYSURA REDDY (Andhra Pradesh): Sir, I would like to draw the attention of 
the Central Government towards the road accidents happening daily in different parts of the 
country. Our Indian roads are very dangerous and insecure. According to reports published 
in the Time of India dated 28th November, 2007, road accidents kill nearly 280 people daily in

India. Among all the Metropolitan cities, 1,717 in Delhi, 1,055 in Chennai, 835 in Bangalore, 
787 in Mumbai, 577 in Hyderabad, 495 in Jaipur, 484 in Kolkata and 598 persons in Kanpur 
have died in road accident's during 2005. In Delhi,  nearly one-fourth of the victims were 
pedestrians. In States, the number of casualities d uring this period is 13,961 in Tamil 
Nadu, 10,944 in Andhra Pradesh, 10616 in Maharashtra, 9,860 in Uttar Pradesh and 6,876 in 
Karnataka. Sir, there are no proper facilities to provide immediate relief to the victims. 
This is a very serious and important matter where the Government should think for safety 
5; and security of the common people in the country. I have observed the rising graph of road 
accidents which is rising steadily since 2005. Neither the State Governments, nor the Central 
Government has taken necessary and effective steps in this direction. In this respect, I would 
like to submit that the accidental deaths in cities and big towns of the country are more than 
the rural areas and villages. 
Therefore, I urge upon the Central Government to formulate a road safety policy for the 
protection, safety and security of the people of the country. Thank you. 
Reqeust to supply required quantities of fertilisers to Andhra Pradesh during 
Rabi Season 
SHRIMATI N.P DURGA (Andhra Pradesh): Sir, the ferti liser consumption in Andhra 
Pradesh is expected to reach 55 lakh tonnes. In spi te of the Fertiliser Monitoring System, 
intended to ensure despatch of fertilisers to distr icts in time, the DAP stocks have not 
reached during the current Kharif Season. The existing agency does not have a wide supply 
network. This hampers the supply. So, at least, for  the Rabi season, there is an immediate 
need to deploy an agency which has wide distributio n network and infrastructure to move 
DAP from ports to retail counters in rural areas of  Andhra Pradesh. The manufacturers of 
complex and SSP fertilisers have drastically brough t down their production due to steep 
increase in the price of raw material, that is. Sul phuric acid, Phosphoric acid and Rock 
Phosphate. 
The requirement of complex and SSP fertilisers is 10.30 lakh tonnes for Rabi, 2007-08, and 
manufacturers have assured only around 6 lakh tonnes. So there is a gap of 4.22 lakh tonnes 
between the demand and supply. Besides there is a s hortage of 1 lakh tonnes of DAP and 
MOP each for the ensuing Rabi. The State has been facing an acute shortage of DAP due to 
slow movement of DAP stocks during Kharif, 2007. 
So in order to prevent delay in supply during the Kharif season, I request the Government 
of India' to arrange for supply of 2.5 lakh tonnes and 1.72 lakh tonnes of complex and SSP 
fertilisers, in addition to the original commitment , to Andhra Pradesh. I also request the 
Government of India to provide one lakh tonnes of DAP and MOP immediately to meet the 
demand. 
Need for Laying of Railway Line from Rupai in Assam to Parshuramkund in 
Arunachal Pradesh  
SHRI NABAM REBIA (Arunachal Pradesh): Sir, the Government of Arunachal Pradesh 
had submitted a proposal with the Ministry of Railw ays for construction of a railway line 
from Rupai in Tinsukia district of Assam to Parshur amkund via. Mahadevpur, Namsai, 
Chongkham and Wakro in  Arunachal Pradesh. 
Arunachal Pradesh is a landlocked State entirely dependent on roads as the only source 
of communication. The tremendous potential of this State and that of its people remained 
untapped for decades due to communication bottleneck. Hence there is a need for a reliable 
communication network to ensure rapid economic growth of this State.

Parshuramkund, located on the left bank of River Lo hit in Arunachal Pradesh, hardly 
120 kms. from Rupai, is the existing nearest rail head in Assam. It is an important religious 
spot and, every year, lakhs of pilgrims throng this  holy spot. Further, the area is extremely 
rich in horticulture products like orange and tea. The proposed railway line will ensure rapid 
economic development of the State. It will also help to transport the goods and equipments 
of BRO, Army, Paramilitary as well as of NHPC, NTPC and other State and Central Government 
agencies. The Government is requested to take up this project on priority.

Need to use electronic mail to communicate courts' judgements  
SHRI SHANTARAM LAXMAN NAIK (Goa): Sir, liberty of an individual being of utmost 
importance is enshrined in the Constitution of Indi a as a fundamental right. This liberty 
cannot be taken away except according to the law of the land. 
Now-a-days, it is seen that convicts are not getting copies of judgements and, as a result 
of which, valuable rights of citizens to seek furth er remedies is delayed and, many a time 
convicts remain in jail for not being able to file appeals/revisions and seek bail. Further, it has 
also been seen that after convicts obtain bail, the y remain in jail on account of non-
communication of the release orders to the jail authorities. 
Sir, when the Government is very keen to increase t he speed of IT revolution in the 
country, and when e-governance is being given top priority and when judiciary is also using 
internet system to a large extent by opening web-sites of various courts, it would have been 
fit and proper that judgements and orders, where li berty of individuals is concerned, 
communication of judgements and orders through e-mails, would have been most ideal. 
It is, therefore, essential that all the jails in this country should have compute systems to 
receive electronic mail, and computers installed therein should have fax receiving software, 
if not separate fax machines.

money, if you spend on health, you can create 20,000, hundred-bed hospitals, quality hospitals 
in this country and meet the health needs of our po pulation. The question is why are we 
going for this expensive option at the expense of k eeping our children illiterate, at the 
expense of not treating those people who require health attention? Why are we going in for 
such an expensive option? This is something for which there is no clear answer so far. The 
other pretext that is given. Sir, so, I think in te rms of cost benefit analysis this is the most 
expensive option we have and as a result of this mo st expensive option we are denying the 
aam aadmi whatever we could have given to him because whenever we say some issues of 
people's welfare must be taken up, there is always this argument that there is a resource 
constraint. If there is a resource constraint, why are we using our scarce resources to satisfy, 
let us say, the orders to multinational corporations in one country, which has not installed a 
new nuclear power reactor in the last two decades? The USA does not install them but it 
wants to sell their nuclear reactors to us. So, we end up buying their nuclear reactors and 
generating profit for them while, in our own country we deprive our own children from going 
to school and getting quality education or our own elderly senior citizens from getting 
quality health attention. Now, this is something no t permissible if we want a real modern 
prosperous India. So, from that point of view, I think, this is a very big folly that we will be 
entering into, and, I think, there must be a re-thi nk done by the Government on this score. 
The other pretext also, Sir they say, is that if we enter the deal, then, we will be breaking the 
nuclear apartheid that is there on India or that we will be sitting on the nuclear high table of

the world. I will come to that later, Sir, because all these are illusions. This is an illusory claim.

claim. Therefore, the pretext for going into this deal, in my opinion, is very faulty and in fact,

If that is the case. Sir, then what is the context in which we have to see this deal? The deal. 
Sir, is not only to be seen in terms of nuclear commerce or the nuclear benefit that is generally 
being propagated. We have the Under Secretary of State of the United States of America who 
has gone on record to state that there are at least  four related benefits to this agreement as 
well. The first concerns non-proliferation. I am quoting. Sir, "For 30 years, India has been on 
the outside of that system, of non-proliferation. With this agreement, India will open up its 
system to international inspection and it puts the majority of its civilian reactors under IAEA 
safeguards. This deal now brings India back into the non-proliferation mainstream in a way 
it was not before." If this is the US claim. Sir, and this is what they want to bring us into, the 
non-proliferation regime through the backdoor, then , all the principled positions that the 
Government of India has taken all along, which we have supported, that we will not sign the 
NPT because it is a discriminatory treaty, all that, falls flat. So, we think that there is a larger 
design that is involved in this deal. The next benefit that he talks about is on the position of, 
and I quote, "The agreement also sends an important  message to nuclear outlaw regimes 
such as Iran" and that is the fact that we have already mentioned a number of times and the 
Hyde Act refers to Iran and our foreign policy positions which have to congruent with what 
the US position will be. The third related benefit he talks about is the fact of military cooperation 
and of military sales. As much as they are interested in 123, Sir, in no unambiguous terms he 
talks of great military commerce with India and their target is 126 and not 123. And 126 is the 
number of combat aircraft, the military aircraft, that we are going to buy and they are hoping 
through this deal that they will cement India into a closer military cooperation. This, again, 
being the case. Sir, what we are now entering into,  in my opinion, is a deal which actually 
takes India closer to the US positions on global is sues as well as on regional strategic 
concerns; and what is being done is to drag India into or suck India into the vortex of being 
a subordinate ally of United States of America; and it is this subordinate ally status which we 
think is not in India's interest at the present moment. Why it is so, I will come to later. But the 
fact remains that this is something which we cannot  afford to do now. I will. Sir, if time 
permits, also refer to certain very derogatory things that have been said about us and about 
our former Prime Ministers by the US Under Secretar y of State. I am quoting, Sir. "The 
benefits of these historic agreements are very real for the United States. For the first time in 
three decades, India will submit its entire nuclear  programme for international inspections 
etc." Secondly, he says that, "If India were to conduct a nuclear test, the United States would 
have the right under US laws to seek the return of all nuclear fuel and technology... Shipped 
by US firms." That apart, the important point on our foreign policy issue is, "This Agreement 
will also send a powerful message to nuclear outlay s like Iran. If you play by the rules as 
India has, you will be rewarded..." — Please underl ine the word 'rewarded' — "...If you do 
not, you will face sanctions and isolation." So, this is the clear message that the US's Official 
Spokesman is saying that India is being rewarded fo r being, as they said, 'playing by the 
rules.' And, who defines the rules — the United Sta tes of America. You play by their rules, 
you will be rewarded. If you do not play by their rules, you will not be rewarded like Iran. That 
is why we have these apprehensions. In the present context, if you look at the pressures that 
are put on India, unfortunately, we think that these pressures are already at work. When the 
Hyde Act talks of Indian Foreign Policy being congruent with that of the United States of

America, where it refers, on three occasions to Ira n, they expect India to toe that line. We

instead of India, the then Dy. Prime Minister, which is on record, says that, in fact, demoaned

and missile defence fields. So, this background, we understand. Sir, is the architecture because if

define as communal forces, away from power. But thi s support was based on a Common

our Foreign Policy direction; where it stated clearly that India will pursue an independent

Foreign Policy, while strengthening relations with all countries, including the USA. There

I had discussed the Hyde Act and its implications in the last debate. We had discussed about

things stated in the Hyde Act were not mandatory fo r him to follow. But, then, remember 
every US President has a right to decide on this. I f, once this President goes and another

provisions can be invoked against India. Let us not  be under any illusion that the present 
President is a great friend of lndia; therefore, being a great friend of India he has said that

fate to befall this Government. Therefore, I ask this Government to seriously reconsider this 
deal and not proceed a head .(lnterruptions)

Now the question is, the respective national law for the United States America is the Hyde

The first one concerns the uninterrupted fuel suppl ies. Yes, the 123 Agreement talks of 
uninterrupted fuel supplies till the life of the re actors. But, once the 123 Agreement is

we will have uninterrupted fuel supplies.

dual use technologies are barred from being transferred to India; whether it is on reprocessing,

agreement is further amended? And the full nuclear cooperation clause, which the hon. Prime 
Minister assured us here, even that is not going to be fulfilled according to this text. 
The third assurance is this. The hon. Prime Minister said that everything should be done

terminated upon the will and whim of the U.S. Presi dent. If that is the case, if that can be 
terminated, why should India be subjected to a perp etual safeguards by the International 
Atomic Energy? If 123 is terminated, then, this also ought to be terminated. That reciprocity

using uranium towards using thorium, there is another intermediate stage that comes where 
plutonium is also used to a certain extent. Now, when you have a Uranium-Plutonium cycle, 
which will lead up to thorium cycle, the moment plutonium comes into the picture, plutonium 
as an input also goes into nuclear weapons. There a re international safeguards you have 
submitted yourselves to; the moment you reach the s tage of plutonium, anybody can raise 
his finger and say, 'Plutonium is generated, you are transferring this to use for your nuclear 
weapons; and, therefore, the safeguards will apply.' You subject yourselves to international 
inspections, including the US inspections. I suspec t and we firmly believe that there is an 
international effort to try and ensure that India does not reach that stage where we can use

thorium as nuclear fuel. If we reach that stage of using thorium as nuclear fuel, then, no

they attempting to do? Sir. To put it in a nutshell, the world, after the bi-polarity of the cold

seriously reconsider the path that they are following. Hold talks with the IAEA, come back 
and let us reconsider this. The hon. Prime Minister  has himself stated in this House in the 
past that before they take any further step, they would come back to the Parliament. This is 
a very healthy trend and we hope that that traditio n will be maintained. Though it didn't 
happen before the 123 Agreement was initialised, ne vertheless, subsequently. Government 
agreed to continue with this discussion. I hope that will be done and they would not take any 
hasty measures to rush into this deed. 
Sir, my respected colleague, Jayaji, has passed on a note to me. I would like to end with

youth under the age of 25 that a new India will be built. It is for that new India that you must 
build your youngsters today. Invest in your youth; do not invest on profits for multi-
national corporations.

rethink to this entire deal and to stop it now, before it is too late and we become victims of 
blandishment, which our country cannot and will not ever want to be.

DR. ABHISHEK MANU SINGHVI (Rajasthan): Mr. Deputy C hairman, Sir, I rise on a 
debate which, Sir, is an unusual amalgam of politics, of economics, of technical jargons, of 
statistical analyses and, indeed, of law. It is a debate. Sir, which has been oozing out of our 
respective ears for so many months, and perhaps, this delayed debate would have dampened 
some interest in it. But the issues are no less important. The issues retain their vital importance. 
And we hope that especially since it is a parliamen tary debate, there will be far less of 
explosion or implosion and far more of fusion and fission, or, at least, far more of light than 
heat. Sir, this is a matter where we should keep out of our mind some premeditated notions 
and approach the subject with a critical enquiring eye and an open mind and then allow the 
power of reason and logic to operate.

Sir, may I say at the outset that this is a good deal for a good and responsible nation by a 
good Government headed by a good Prime Minister? It is a key which unlocks the door not 
only to a large hall but indeed to the universe. It  turns us from * outcasts to mainstream 
players. And, Sir, we have to judge it not by what we may imagine or dream about; we have 
to judge it not by somebody's fanciful imagination, but by what we can get, what we have 
got. Sir, we cannot allow the perfect to be the enemy of the good. I shall endeavour. Sir, to 
deal with each of the issues; important, less important, boring, more sensatiortal, as made by 
the hon. previous speakers whom I have heard with rapt attention. So, let me start. Sir, with 
the issue of energy security made by my friend, Mr. Yechury. Sir, the basic point on energy 
security is that there is no one source of energy o n which we can give more focus or more 
importance. The approach has to be multi-pronged, multi-faceted, and holistic. And that is 
the complete error, that is the fundamental error, of the arguments which have gone by earlier 
regarding energy security. Sir, as somebody has said, statistics can be misleading like certain 
articles of clothing. What they reveal is interesti ng, what they conceal is vital. But, Sir, 
statistics can be instructive. Let us start with the per-capita energy consumption; — and we 
measure this in a special measure called KGOE, Kilogram of Oil Equivalent. For India, the 
KGOE is roughly 515. Sir, that is 16 times less than the US; it is nine times less than Japan; it 
is eight times less than UK and it is less than many, many other countries in the world, and, 
of course, of the countries which have nuclear power, we rank almost in the last two or three, 
globally. Now, the argument made is that at the end of the day, if we have nuclear power, we 
will have only seven per cent. Six per cent is what Mr. Yechury says. The correct figure is 
seven per cent. He forgets that even seven per cent would be roughly, — and this is only by 
2020, — over 30,000 megawatts, which is an eight-fo ld increase. It would still be a small 
percentage because by then our other sources of ene rgy would also be growing. When 
other sources grow, the nuclear component percentag e will remain small. But that is no 
reason not to have it. Let me give you a startling statistic. In all of our last two or three Five 
Year Plans, the capacity addition of electricity has been half of what we have projected. We 
have the figures for the earlier. Plans, and in each Plan the actual capacity added by us is half 
of what we have projected. Now, Sir, if we will have 30,000 MW by 2020 through this deal, if 
you extrapolate the total amount of energy by 2050 or 2045, the Planning Commission estimates 
it to be about 1.3 million MW. There is no reason why by 2050, out of the total 1.3 million MW, 
we should not have 10,15,20 per cent by nuclear sources. And, what would be 20 per cent of 
that? Sir, 20 per cent of that would be the very impressive figure of 2.6 lakh megawatts from 
nuclear energy. Today's figure is something like 3000 MW. Therefore, the fact that you have 
energy from other sources, and that you should purs ue energy from other sources, cannot 
ever mean a lackadaisical approach on energy regard ing nuclear sources. Why is it that 
countries like France—of course, it has a very high  percentage—countries like Belgium, 
Sweden, Switzerland and Japan have a high percentage? The lowest figures are 20 per cent 
for the USA and the UK, 20 per cent being the figur e of the total energy met from nuclear 
sources. These countries are not foolish, these countries are not suicidal. Belgium has 60 per 
cent, Sweden has 42 per cent, Switzerland has 39 per cent. But the minimum figure, the lower 
figures for the US, and the UK are still 20 per cent! So, if we aspire to jumpstart our figures to 
6 or 7 per cent, what is wrong in that?

If 55 per cent of the global energy increase is from 2005 to 2030,45 per cent out of a total

Sir, let me turn to costs; it is good to look at costs; it is important to look at costs. But, Sir, 
just to digress for a moment, the price of crude oil in 1973 was roughly 2 USS per barrel. Last 
month, it was 75 USS per barrel. Well, do my friends ever talk of the price of oil? Do they talk 
of the cost of oil? (Interruptions) Let me come to that, I have not reached that. Have some 
patience. I am only starting with the price of oil which you, my friends, have been using in 
this country for the last 30 years at an unaffordable cost. It increases every day. You have no 
control over it. It is usually an imported item. You have hardly any indigenous sources, but 
oil is the mainstay of our consumption. We will come to nuclear energy cost in a moment. 
Let me talk about the cost. No doubt a coal plant is cheaper at the initial cost. It incidentally 
has a life of only 25-30 years and, let me tell you, a nuclear plant has 40-50-year life-cycle, but 
no doubt, a coal plant is cheaper as far as the initial capital cost is concerned. But two points 
here. Coal is a very transport-intensive product. By the time it reaches you, at what is called 
the load-centre where you and I can use it, the cos t of coal—that is, the relevant cost of 
coal—comes to around Rs.3 per unit.

Secondly, coal is highly polluting. You do not add the cost of pollution; you do not add 
the cost of transport. As against that nuclear, first of all, nuclear is not 11 crores, the figure 
given by the previous speakers. If you buy nuclear plants from other parts of the world than 
the USA, it can be significantly cheaper in the region of 8 to 9 crores. But more important than 
that, the only statistical study published about nu clear plant cost is a study published by 
Mr. Grover of the DAE. It is a statistical study of  19 countries, which has published and 
proved that nuclear plants are the cheapest if you even count a 20-year cycle. And remember, 
a cycle of a nuclear plant is 50 years; the cycle of a coal plant is 20 to 30 years. Let me give you 
the four conclusions of the study by Dr. Grover published. The report gives ratios on a study 
in which 19 countries participated. And if you take a lower discount rate of only 5 per cent— 
I am reading from the report — nuclear power is che aper as compared to gas in all the 19 
countries. Secondly, if you take coal except for South Korea and the USA, nuclear power is
